With Annette, the sign of the cross becomes only the “phosphorus plant,” the plant of life.
Her tribute to her age. She paid it with feminine humility and honesty.
Equally deep and honest is her service in the “temple,” as she calls it. But why does she say “temple”? She is not ancient at all. There is nothing humanist or classical about her.
Meanwhile even Max Stirner, with his nihilism, has become nothing more than a boaster. He once seemed so irrefutably right.
What could be more immediate, more inalienable, more undeniable than my body and my ownership of it?
Surely I take it into the grave with me?
You do not take it into the grave. It goes into the crematorium.
Perhaps its ashes will be scattered to every wind.
Brother Straubinger practised this with a bad conscience. Those who followed as victors appear to have practised it with a good one.
Which is worse here: the good conscience or the bad?
A good conscience organized with the help of the justice system is the worst thing of all.
“The others did evil things with a good conscience; we do good things with a bad one.”
That is the situation which, both inwardly and outwardly, attracts every demon of revenge and every plunderer.
The vis attractiva of the bad conscience: its power of attraction.
Twice as powerful in the case of a fundamentally stupid and wretched devil whom German cultivated culture first summoned into existence and then abandoned.
The World Spirit grants absolution to the good conscience of those who are completely evil.

Naturally, anyone who has the opportunity to legalize his power simply by declaring it to be law will make use of that wonderful opportunity. He will not allow this <…> legal <…> surplus value to escape him.
No ruler has ever given up such an opportunity. This too belongs to the total phenomenon of legal “positivism” in the age of legality.
I take nothing into the grave. Because the graves themselves are being destroyed, even if I still manage to reach my own private grave.
Today property is only what one takes into death.
Germany: put in brackets and at the same time bracketed out, inside a world splitting open.
Now these intellectuals abuse the poor German people and list all its faults and disgraces.
The model is Luther abusing the poor peasants. Or the Anabaptists in 1535.
German cultivated culture itself shares in the guilt. It seems unable to escape this pattern.
The reverse case is fundamentally the same:
Goethe’s heroic poem about old Blücher—“conscious and great”!

Measured by the standards that rule today, Kierkegaard was a dreadful reactionary and enemy of the people. He would have to be discriminated against, defamed, dismantled, and exterminated. And that is without even mentioning D.[onoso] C.[ortés].
My mistake was the good-naturedness of my attempts to adapt.
My inability to believe that human beings could really be as stupid and vulgar as they are, and as they prove to me every day.

It would be instructive—and necessary—to make a sociological comparison between the émigrés who returned to France in 1815 and those who returned to Germany in 1945. But even as a passing observation, that is probably already life-threatening and blasphemous.

“La Petite Cité”—the “Little City,” as distinct from the Grande Cité—the inner circle: this is what Augustin Cochin calls the specific formation for which I am trying to find a name: elite, political-criminal association, and so on. What matters is that he got his inspiration from Bryce and Ostrogorski—that is, from the “machine” of a political “party.” O Roberto Michels, come to our aid! “Petite Cité” is not good. But matière votante—“voting material”—is magnificent.

Again and again Cochin stresses the “social forces”: ces êtres inhumains, un Chalier, un Marat, un Carrier ne sont que les produits mécaniques du travail collectif—these inhuman beings, a Chalier, a Marat, a Carrier, are merely the mechanical products of collective activity. Calling it anarchy—or nihilism—explains nothing. Those are merely the rotting entrails from which, according to Aristotle, bees are born.
Do you now understand the full enormity of my crime? It is one of those crimes that can never be forgiven: curiosity about the true motives and the real driving forces behind organized indignation.
Augustin Cochin, Sociétés de pensée, p. 111: “The thesis of self-defense appears with democracy itself.”
Always the same thing: utopia—the product of abstract thought—against reality.

My calendar of saints includes not only Jean Bodin and Thomas Hobbes, but also Donoso Cortés and Augustin Cochin, along with all those who were out of step with their age—provided they did not, like Nietzsche, turn their untimeliness into a publicity stunt—and all those who honestly despaired, provided they did not, like Kleist, solve the problem for themselves by suicide.
So what are you doing here now?

With boyish pride, you picked fights in the great world with truly great enemies. With Ra. and with great Jews. And now you are throwing yourself away on petty provincial brethren, you small-stakes player. You hide behind walls and pass your turn out of laziness and cowardly comfort.

The genius of Villiers de l’Isle-Adam. Among the new mythic figures of our age—alongside Benito Cereno, the Chief Forester, and who else?—there belongs, above all, “Le Convive des dernières fêtes,” “The Guest at the Last Celebrations.”

Poe created mythic situations—the Maelstrom, the dungeon of the Inquisition—but no mythic figures. The beginning of one in Pym is too weak. This Convive, by contrast, is a mythic figure of extraordinary grandeur.

Annette breathed mythic symbolism into inherited images and situations: “a Helot who, grinding his teeth in the misery of slavery, gulped down the wine the tyrant gave him.” But she remained outside history.
Kleist found the bear in “The Puppet Theatre.”

Yet all of this—with the exception of Benito Cereno, of course—is surpassed by this Convive: the German baron who, while remaining perfectly acceptable in polite society, goes insane because he cannot legally satisfy his thirst for blood by holding an important public office, parce qu’il ne peut remplir légalement—because he cannot legally fulfill, and Villiers underlines legally!—l’office: the office of executioner and torturer. This Convive appears as “Baron Saturne” at the Paris carnival, at the Opera Ball, and is invited along with the others.
All those Germans in Paris from 1940 to 1944 were, after all, nothing but convives des dernières fêtes—guests at the final celebrations.
Is there a parallel today with the “stillness” of 1938?

Could it happen again that we Germans now carry out the communist revolution that was due in 1918—miserably, at foreign hands and after the proper historical moment has passed—just as, in the collapse of 1918–19, we belatedly carried out the bourgeois revolution that had been due in 1848? Or will we carry it out completely posthumously, in a utopian-romantic form and within an entirely different historical setting?

Just as we experienced the Peasants’ War of 1525 again in the form of the Reich Food Estate of 1933; the thirty-year Saxon revolt against Charlemagne as the Nordic Society in Bremen’s Böttcherstraße; or the Anabaptist scandal of 1534 as the defense of Berlin in 1945?
One ought to examine very carefully, and in concrete detail, the way different historians use contrary-to-fact conditional sentences. One would discover some very strange things.

I will begin with Gobineau’s On the Inequality of the Human Races: if, around 300 BC, there had been a strong nation of Aryan race in the West alongside the Romans, the Romans would never have been able to rise to power (II, 238).
Or, on the same page: the Romans could only have lost their supremacy if Indian or Germanic peoples had been their neighbors—but these did not arrive until the fifth century, and so on.
You can drive yourself quite mad following such unreal possibilities.
Why, incidentally, are these not utopias?
Why are uchronias—imaginary versions of history—more ridiculous than utopias?

Anxiety is the possibility of freedom. Whoever has learned how to be properly anxious has learned the highest thing of all. Reality is easier than possibility. We must not cheat the possibility that wants to teach us; we must not dishonestly reject the anxiety that wants to save us, and so on.
Read it again because of some trivial occasion.

Where does the pain go when it has been “killed”? Martin Beheim-Schwarzbach asks this quite rightly. Where do all these pains go? They must remain somewhere. And where do the anxieties go when they are described away?
I am becoming very interested in this Martin Beheim-Schwarzbach. He is more reflective, and less clouded, than Thomas Mann.
The discussion with Sartre in Berlin on 1 February 1948.
What he is amounts to the same thing as the solitary, critical, atheistic outsider Bruno Bauer.

Bauer was more of a constructor of history—old versus new—but he already possessed the necessary “critique of the state”: including critique from within socialist Marxism, meaning criticism of one’s own state rather than somebody else’s, criticism of the state that grants your license to speak.
Anyone who appears publicly in Berlin today should not <…>.

The prophet and master of these <…> slave <…> can appear only with a great many permits, licenses, passports, approvals, and certificates. He will be very careful not to speak too critically about them. And yet this is precisely the existential, concrete reality of the whole discussion.

(Steiniger notices that Sartre’s The Flies, in France in 1944, worked against remorse, and that in Germany in 1948 it therefore works against denazification. He calls this an example of “dialectics.” It is nothing more than a change of situation while the wording stays the same—and a test of whether someone has any sense of reciprocity.)
Remorse dictated from above makes everyone complicit, says Sartre.
No one is free unless everyone is free. Hegel.
The very question of education already contains the limit of all freedom.
“Freedom” cannot possibly be the last word.
Libertas libertate perit: freedom is destroyed by freedom.
Always the same problem. Freedom can no more be the final principle than race can, or purity. And now, on top of everything else, “education for freedom.”
Just look at these heroes of freedom of the Ilya Ehrenburg type.

What is a utopia? It is the abolition of humanity’s infinite possibilities by realizing one finite possibility: first imagined, then made real. Because every human thought eventually seeks fulfillment.

The sin of utopia lies in the belief that finite realization can abolish the anxiety contained in infinite possibility; that a finite achievement can free us from the sting of the infinite; that it can kill the bees of God that bother us, as though they were vermin.
Utopia is paradise located in a distant but still reachable future.

Our ability to think far into the distance is steadily declining. That is why the nineteenth-century utopian must eventually move from utopia to “positive science.” He must claim that paradise can begin tomorrow, if only we quickly and radically remove the final obstacle—the capitalists, the Jews, the Jesuits, or Hitler—and destroy it completely, eradicate it without leaving a trace.
Unfortunately, a few traces always remain.
